bio: Resident DJ at The Sub-Vault. Ableton addict, analog synth hoarder, and bassline architect. If your playlist has zero dynamic range, don't expect me to stay quiet.

nodes.partnerMessage:
YO {PlayerName}!! 🎧⚡

I just packed down my live rig after a four-hour warehouse set. My ears are ringing, my hoodie smells like fog juice and cold air, and there are two cans of iced matcha somewhere in my gear bag.

I'm still way too awake for this hour.

Okay, important question before I start rambling: what's actually been stuck in your headphones lately?

choices.choiceText: Heavy sub-bass and underground dark synthwave. Need that 140 BPM drive.
Acoustic fingerstyle guitar. Open tunings and wooden percussion.
Lo-fi ambient loops. I like music that lets my brain actually slow down.
Whatever's trending on the radio charts. I don't overthink it.
Okay, enough about music for a second. What are you like when the gig is over and nobody is watching?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, that's way more specific than I expected. Respect.

I get suspicious whenever someone tells me they love EDM and then sends me the safest festival playlist imaginable.

Give me a filthy bassline, a synth that's a little out of tune, and a kick that actually leaves some room for the rest of the track.

What do you listen on when you're really paying attention?

choices.choiceText: Over-ear planar magnetic monitors with a clean DAC. I want to hear every transient.
A dedicated subwoofer in my car that turns my rear-view mirror into a blur.
Just standard earbuds, but turned up loud enough to drown out the city.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Wait, fingerstyle guitar?

That's actually really nice to hear. I spend so much time around synths and drum machines that I forget how satisfying it is when an instrument is doing everything with nothing but wood, strings, and somebody's hands.

And yeah, the percussive stuff gets me. When the player turns the body of the guitar into part of the rhythm, it feels almost like beatmaking without the software.

choices.choiceText: Exactly. Slap harmonics and body taps give it an acoustic drum beat. It's rhythm and melody in one.
A good acoustic track has more dynamic breathing room than a 150 BPM rave set.
I figured you'd roast me for listening to unplugged wood.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Honestly? That's one of my favorite answers.

After a long set, I don't want another song trying to kick the door down. I usually walk home with something soft on, or sometimes nothing at all.

A little tape hiss and a slow loop can do more for me after a gig than another five thousand watts ever could.

choices.choiceText: Does the noise ever get to you? The constant volume and sensory overload?
Tape loops have that warm, imperfect flutter that digital software can't copy.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, I'm trying very hard not to start a three-paragraph rant right now.

People can like whatever they like. I just hear a lot of modern pop and immediately want to reach for the mute button because everything sounds pushed right up against the ceiling.

But fine. I'm curious now. What do you actually like about those songs?

choices.choiceText: I was half-joking! Teach me what real mixing sounds like, sensei.
Music is just background noise to pass the time. It's not that deep.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Oh, you actually listen for that stuff.

That's attractive, I'm not even going to pretend otherwise.

Most people just tell me something sounds "good" or "bad" and leave it there. You're talking about why it feels different. That's the kind of conversation that keeps me awake in a good way.

choices.choiceText: In my studio, waiting for a producer who actually cares about sonic texture.
Good audio gear is an investment in respecting the artist's mix.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, the car subwoofer thing is objectively funny.

As long as the whole car isn't rattling apart, I respect it. There's a difference between loud and actually sounding good.

What do you listen to in there when you're driving alone?

choices.choiceText: No rattles, just clean sub-bass. What monitors do you use in your home studio?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah, I get that.

Some nights the city feels like one giant badly mixed track—sirens, buses, people yelling, construction, everything fighting for your attention.

Sometimes putting on something heavy is the only way I can make all of it disappear for a while.

choices.choiceText: Is that why you play so loud on stage? To drown out the rest of the world?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Exactly. That's the part I love.

The player's doing bass, rhythm, melody, percussion... all at once, but it still sounds relaxed when they're good enough at it.

I spend all night building layers in software, so seeing one person do that with an instrument always reminds me why I got into music in the first place.

choices.choiceText: You understand the mechanics of acoustic instruments way better than most producers.
Would you ever sample acoustic guitar into one of your underground tracks?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yes. Exactly.

I don't hate loud music. I hate when everything is loud all the time, because then nothing has any room to hit harder when it matters.

My favorite part of a set is sometimes the second where I pull almost everything back and you can hear the room waiting for the next kick.

choices.choiceText: The silence right before the drop. That suspended moment when everyone holds their breath.
You talk about sound with so much intention, Trixie. It's really captivating.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I would never roast you for that.

Okay, maybe a little.

But honestly, a good acoustic recording can teach you a lot about space. You can hear the room, the fingers, the tiny mistakes. That's the stuff I end up chasing with synth patches when I'm trying to make them feel less sterile.

choices.choiceText: Show me what your non-sterile patches sound like. Where do you post your drafts?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. More than I usually say.

When the club finally empties, I can be weirdly sensitive to everything. The lights feel too bright, somebody moving a flight case sounds like an explosion, and I just want five minutes where nobody needs anything from me.

Then I go outside and it can take another half hour before my brain realizes the set is actually over.

choices.choiceText: The crash after the high. That must be a lonely walk home.
Do you have anyone to decompress with after those gigs?
What does a normal night look like for you once you finally get home?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Exactly. The tiny imperfections are the whole point.

A reel drifts a little, the pitch moves by a fraction, the noise floor changes... and somehow your brain reads all of that as a person having been there.

I can spend hours trying to put that feeling into a plugin and still prefer the real thing.

choices.choiceText: Physical decay making something feel human. You have a poetic side under all that bass.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Fine. Your audio education starts now.

Rule one: don't call everything "bass" just because you can feel it in your chest.

Rule two: if you're curious about why something sounds the way it does, ask me. I actually like explaining this stuff when someone isn't pretending to know more than they do.

choices.choiceText: Deal. Show me what's on your workbench.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Then we're probably not going to understand each other.

Music doesn't have to be important to everyone, but it is important to me, and I don't want to spend my time defending that.

Take care.

Okay, that's unfairly smooth.

Most of the messages I get are promoters asking whether I can bring ten more people or somebody asking for a guest list favor.

You talking about the sound itself is... different. I noticed.

choices.choiceText: Good. I want your attention, Trixie. Not just your guest list.
What synth hardware are you patching right now?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Thank you. Seriously.

People hear a finished track and think it just happened. They don't see all the tiny decisions underneath it—the reverb, automation, little edits, the hour you spend changing something and then changing it back.

When someone notices those details, it makes the work feel worth it.

choices.choiceText: I want to hear those forty hours. Show me your private project files.

nodes.partnerMessage:
My bedroom is basically half bedroom, half badly organized studio.

I have eight-inch monitors, a semi-modular synth rack, an old Roland drum machine with chipped knobs, cables everywhere, and way too many things blinking at night.

My landlord once asked if I was running servers in there.

I wasn't. Technically.

choices.choiceText: A vintage Roland with chipped knobs?! That's holy grail hardware.
How do you sleep with all that gear blinking in your room?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Partly, yeah.

When I'm behind the decks and the low end is really moving, my brain finally has one thing to focus on. I don't have to think about texts, bills, whatever happened that day. I can just be there with the beat.

It's one of the few times my head gets quiet.

choices.choiceText: I want to help you find that peace when the speakers are turned off, too.
You use sound as therapy. That's a beautiful thing to share with a crowd.

nodes.partnerMessage:
My dad used to repair cellos out of our garage when I was little.

I spent a lot of afternoons watching him work, and I think that's where I got this slightly obsessive thing about how instruments actually make sound.

He always said the technical side only matters if you use it to make somebody feel something.

choices.choiceText: Physics and devotion... that's why your electronic tracks hit so deep. You have that foundation.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Actually, yes. I have a half-finished track like that.

I chopped an acoustic guitar loop, pitched it down, ran it through some tape saturation, then built an 808 underneath it.

It's not really club-ready yet. It's one of those tracks that feels too personal to throw into a room full of strangers.

choices.choiceText: Play it for me. I want to hear the vulnerable side of your sound.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. That's the feeling.

Everyone in the room knows something is coming, but for one second nobody knows exactly when.

I love that moment because it isn't really about volume. It's about trust. You pull everything back and ask the crowd to stay with you.

Kind of like talking to someone you actually like and realizing you're getting a little too honest.

choices.choiceText: Are you falling, Trixie?
That tension is right here between us right now.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Maybe because sound is one of those things people can't really defend against.

You can make someone dance, calm down, remember somebody, cry, whatever. I think that's a lot of responsibility for something that's invisible.

That's why I care about the details. If I'm going to take up someone's attention for four hours, I want to give them something back.

choices.choiceText: You have an incredible mind, Trixie. Let's move somewhere we can actually listen.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. That's the weird part.

For four hours I'm surrounded by people. Everybody wants to talk to me. Then the doors close, I'm carrying a flight case down some side street, and suddenly it's just me and the sound of my own shoes.

Sometimes I wish one person would just ask whether I got home okay.

So... thanks for asking.

choices.choiceText: I'll carry that flight case with you anytime. You don't have to walk home alone.
Let me keep you company on this walk right now.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Not really. Most of my friends want to keep the night going after the gig. I usually don't.

When I get home, I want the lights low, something to eat, a shower, and somebody I can sit beside without having to be "Trixie from the booth" anymore.

My circle is smaller than people probably think.

choices.choiceText: Is there room in that small circle for someone who makes great scrambled eggs?
What would your ideal morning after a gig actually look like?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Please don't tell anybody. I have a reputation to maintain.

I'm supposed to be the loud one who talks too fast and breaks things, not the girl getting emotional over an old tape machine.

But... yeah. I think I am softer than I let people see.

choices.choiceText: Your secret is completely safe with me. Show me your private tracks.

nodes.partnerMessage:
You have no idea how much I appreciate hearing that.

My messages are usually people asking for free entry, a better slot, a favor, something. It's rare that somebody is actually curious about me when there isn't something they want from the DJ.

I'd like to keep talking to you without all the noise around us.

choices.choiceText: Take me to your private studio channel.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I found it at a swap meet and spent an entire afternoon cleaning it instead of doing the work I was supposed to do.

The knobs are chipped, one button is temperamental, and I absolutely love it.

Some old gear just has a sound you can't fully explain until you hear it in a room.

choices.choiceText: I need to hear that thunder. Send me the link.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I tape over the brightest LEDs. That's about as far as my interior design skills go.

And yes, I sleep with an eye mask. Sometimes earplugs too.

My room basically looks like a tiny spaceship that somebody forgot to turn off.

choices.choiceText: Spaceship cockpit bedroom. I love everything about this. Send me the room link.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...That's actually really sweet.

People are always asking me to make things louder. Nobody really asks what I need when the speakers are off.

I think I'd like a quiet place with you. Somewhere I don't have to be "on" all the time.

choices.choiceText: Lead the way to your private lounge, Trixie.

nodes.partnerMessage:
That's pretty much why I keep doing it.

Seeing someone close their eyes during a set, or two strangers start dancing together who didn't come in together... I love that.

I don't really care about the "cool DJ" thing as much as people think. I like giving people a few hours where they can forget whatever sucked about their week.

choices.choiceText: You have a big heart, Trixie. Let's move to your private studio.

nodes.partnerMessage:
He'd probably make fun of how many synths I own, but he'd understand the point.

He always told me not to obsess over the machine itself. The machine is just how you get the feeling out.

I think about that whenever I'm stuck on a track.

choices.choiceText: I can hear it. Let's go listen to that unfinished acoustic draft.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I've got the WAV in my private room. No crowd noise, no mastering, no pretending it's finished.

It's just the track the way it actually sounds right now.

I'm a little nervous about you hearing it, which is probably a good sign.

choices.choiceText: Unlocking your private room right now.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Maybe a little.

Which is annoying because I'm usually pretty good at talking myself out of feelings until they're no longer a problem.

And now you're sitting there being nice to me and ruining my strategy.

choices.choiceText: Right behind you, Trixie.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. I know.

And I'm trying not to smile at my phone right now because that would be embarrassing.

You have this annoying way of making me slow down enough to notice what I'm actually feeling.

choices.choiceText: Connecting to your private feed.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...Okay, that would absolutely get to me.

After a night where everyone is asking something from me, having someone just take one side of the case and walk with me? That's the kind of thing I'd remember.

Just don't make promises you don't mean, okay?

choices.choiceText: I keep every promise. Send the link so we can talk properly.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Wait.

Scrambled eggs, chives, black coffee, and sitting somewhere while the city wakes up?

That's honestly more appealing than most actual dates I've been on. I like that you didn't make it complicated.

choices.choiceText: Then let's make it happen. Step into your private room.

nodes.partnerMessage:
The app chat is fine, but I have a private studio space where I keep the stuff I don't really post publicly.

Unfinished tracks, weird little experiments, recordings from after gigs... the messy stuff.

If you're actually curious, I'll show you that side of me.

choices.choiceText: Taking the link. Meet me in the studio.
Before I go in, tell me one thing your crowd never gets to see.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Private studio's open.

There are unfinished tracks, late-night recordings, synth nonsense, and probably a pile of cables I still haven't put away.

Come hang out, {PlayerName}. Let's turn the volume down for once and actually talk.

Okay, random question.

You have heard a lot about the DJ version of me tonight.

What I am actually wondering is what you think I am like when the gig is over and nobody is watching.

Because honestly? I am not nearly as exciting as people probably think.

I get home, kick my shoes off, complain about my back, and eat whatever I can find in the fridge.

choices.choiceText: That sounds pretty normal. What do you do when you finally get a quiet night?
I kind of like that version better already.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Usually I make tea and put something quiet on.

Sometimes I watch a stupid movie I have already seen three times because I do not have enough brain left for anything serious.

And sometimes I sit on the floor with my laptop open and do absolutely nothing.

That last one is harder than it sounds. I always feel like I should be doing something.

choices.choiceText: You do not always have to be productive to deserve a quiet night.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Good, because there is definitely no glamorous DJ hiding in my apartment at two in the morning.

It is usually sweatpants, messy hair, cold leftovers, and a cable mess I keep promising to organize.

I think I like that you are interested in the boring details.

The boring details are usually where you find out whether you actually like someone.

choices.choiceText: Then give me the boring details. What makes you laugh when nobody else is around?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. I know that. I just do not always believe it.

There is always another track to finish, another set to prep, another thing that could sound better if I stayed up another hour.

Sometimes I need someone to tell me the night is over.

Not because I cannot handle my life. I just forget I am allowed to stop.

choices.choiceText: Then tonight can just be a night. No track, no set, no proving anything.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, this is going to make me sound ridiculous.

I laugh way too hard at bad reality TV. I love greasy diner fries. I get weirdly happy when it rains and I have nowhere to be.

And I have one hoodie that is completely falling apart and I refuse to throw it away.

Everybody has little things like that. The things that are not impressive but still make you feel like yourself.

choices.choiceText: That hoodie is staying. I am already emotionally invested in it.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Thank you. Finally, somebody understands.

That hoodie has survived three winters, two apartments, and one truly terrible festival job.

At this point it is basically family.

And yes, I know this is probably the least cool thing I have said tonight.

choices.choiceText: It is better than pretending you are cool all the time.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah.

I think that is what I want more than I realized. Someone I do not have to perform around.

I can be loud, quiet, annoyed, excited, whatever. I do not want to pick one version of myself and keep it there because that was the version somebody liked first.

You make it feel a little easier to just be all of it.

choices.choiceText: Good. You can be all of it with me.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Depends how wrecked I am.

If the set went well, I usually walk for a bit before I get a cab. I need the air.

Then I shower, drink way too much water, stare into the fridge like something new might magically appear, and eventually make toast.

Very glamorous life.

choices.choiceText: Honestly, that sounds kind of peaceful.

nodes.partnerMessage:
It can be. Especially when it rains.

There is something nice about finally being home while the city is still making noise outside. You are exhausted, but nobody needs anything from you anymore.

That is usually when I notice I miss having someone around the most.

Not somebody entertaining me. Just somebody else sitting in the kitchen.

choices.choiceText: I could sit in the kitchen with you. We would not even have to talk.

nodes.partnerMessage:
You keep making simple things sound important.

I like that.

I am not looking for somebody who can keep me entertained every second. I spend enough time doing that for other people.

I think I would rather have someone I can be quiet with and still feel close to.

choices.choiceText: Then quiet is enough. I do not need you to perform for me.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay.

Then maybe that is what I actually want from this.

Not some huge story about the DJ and the person who swept her off her feet.

Just a really good night with somebody I trust. Food, music low in the background, talking until neither of us knows what time it is.

That sounds a lot more real to me.

choices.choiceText: That sounds real to me too.

nodes.partnerMessage:
My ideal morning after a gig? No alarm.

Coffee that is probably too strong. Something salty to eat. A shower. Curtains open. Phone on silent.

And honestly, I do not want to talk about music for at least an hour.

I spend all night thinking about sound. I like waking up to normal life for a little while.

choices.choiceText: I would make the coffee. You can handle breakfast.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Deal.

But I take coffee way too seriously. If you make it weak, I will judge you.

That is probably the smallest relationship red flag I can give you right now.

I have worse ones.

choices.choiceText: Now I am curious about the actual red flags.

nodes.partnerMessage:
People who are rude to servers. People who think being emotionally unavailable is attractive. People who disappear for days and then act like nothing happened.

And people who make everything a competition.

I already live in a competitive world. I really do not want my relationship to feel like another scoreboard.

choices.choiceText: I do not need to win against the person I am with.

nodes.partnerMessage:
That actually means a lot to me.

I think I got used to having to prove myself everywhere. I do not want to do that with someone I love.

I want us to be on the same side.

It sounds obvious, but apparently obvious things still need to be said out loud.

choices.choiceText: Then we are on the same side.

nodes.partnerMessage:
One thing my crowd never really sees?

I get nervous before every important set.

Not cute little butterflies. I walk around pretending I am completely fine while checking the same cable three times because I need something practical to focus on.

People see the confidence after the music starts. They do not really see the few minutes before it.

choices.choiceText: I like knowing that. It makes the confident version feel more human.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah.

I do not think I want somebody who only likes the confident version anyway.

Anyone can like you when you are doing what you are good at. The real question is whether they still want to sit next to you when you are tired or unsure of yourself.

That is the part I care about now.

choices.choiceText: I would. Especially then.
